Like I had an amendment in the summer that said, before we fund something, $300 million that was going to go to Ukraine, just define the mission. Tell us the mission. And we only get 129 votes, but at least we forced a vote. It didn't pass, obviously. But how do you hold the State Department accountable for success or failure if they don't have to define the mission that they're trying to achieve? paint the target on after you've taken the shot, you can make it look pretty good or pretty bad depending on what your objective is, right? And so we have to define that up front and frankly unless you tell me what the mission is, I don't truly know what resources you need. And so there tends to be this idea that Congress is supposed to just shut up and cut the checks and then let the executive branch do that. That's not our system of government. But a lot of this has gone on under that sort of false premise. I think the other thing is because the public doesn't trust Congress, in part because of the past behavior here, The public largely supports a strong executive solution when it comes to threats to national security. They know that in general somebody can at least be decisive. Right now is a window of opportunity because they know that in general the Biden administration is very weak and we're being taken advantage of on every front. They know that even the exit out of Afghanistan was terrible. You don't have to have served in the military to know that first you get the civilians out and then you take the military out. The Biden administration did that the wrong way. And that is their issue. The Trump administration didn't commit to how to get out of Afghanistan. They just said, we're going to get out. And so I think the opportunity is for Congress to update our authorizations for military force to expire everything and to start anew And one of the limiting factors we should do is every Congress should have to vote, right? You force a vote every Congress, and that's how you know the country is still committed to this. They're committed to it in a different way, or they're no longer committed to it. And a lot of people say, well, that's a date certain to fail. No, why would you assume that it's going to fail? The default is Congress always says, yeah, let's have more wars in more places so far. It's rare that Congress turns off anything. They just keep cutting the checks. But the reality is you should have a way that you know every Congress is going to at least vote on this. So nothing should extend past each Congress. So we're in the 118th. If we want something that like the War on Terror probably will continue for a long time. Well, the 119th, if they want to stay waging it the same way, they have to vote. And if they want to change something, that vote is the leverage to force some change. And those are features that bipartisan coalition do agree on. And hopefully, as we review those, we can actually get that to become the law.

speaker: SPEAKER_02
transcript: I think it's a good question. It is interesting that some of our biggest warharks aren't people who served. And frankly, I suspect wouldn't serve. But nevertheless, lots of people who did serve their default position is to support more engagement than I have supported. And I'll tell you one of the things that really is top of mind for me is when I served in 75th Ranger Regiment, I had one of my soldiers who had served in Ranger Regiment when they were involved in Moby-Dishu Somalia. And after six Rangers got killed, there were others that were killed there too, but six people from his unit were killed, the United States left. They got out of Somalia and kind of backed off of that for a time. And he's like, if we went over there and did what we had to do, which involved returning fire against people who were using women as human shields, you can't delete those files. This guy's got that in his brain for life, right? So he's normal. He wrestles with that. It's hard to say you had to participate in something where that was involved. And it was the right decision. He asked me, did I make the right decision? Absolutely you did. If you didn't return fire, your own unit would have been killed. Maybe you would have been killed. You had to return fire to break contact from them. And that was the right thing to do. Their own friends, family members, neighbors are the ones that put them at risk, not you. He wrestled with that. And he's like, if we were going to do all those things, why did we quit? Why did we go in the first place? And I think that's why you owe it to the people that are going to wage our nation's wars to at least vote. You're going to send them into harm's way. You're going to ask this of them. You should at least vote. And I think when you do vote, And Congress does its job, just like the founders intended, then the country is at war. And yeah, the countries that were either way, but it's pretty passive on behalf of Congress. So you ask this of people by continuing to cut the checks, but you want to ignore those tough things. And I think that's part of it. People don't want to be held accountable to account or have to wrestle with the tough decisions that people do on the battlefield. And my colleagues, if they're going to cut a check for that, They ought to have to vote on it.

speaker: SPEAKER_02
transcript: Yeah, I'm grateful I had kind of given up hope on having the response. I was able to eventually have a conversation with Secretary Blinken that produced, I think, his response to this letter. And it's like, hey, I've been waiting for quite a while for an answer. And so we had a conversation and in short order after that, I did get the letter. And look, I don't agree with all that I think the State Department's implying with that response. And the part that's left unsaid, I mean, you know, you know, go back to, you know, I think Frederick Posty, that's the guy that what's seen versus unseen. And, you know, kind of the extension of that's what's said and what's unsaid is really NATO membership. I think that a lot of the US national security apparatus, a lot of NATO and therefore the European Union's national security apparatus sees it as is Ukraine part of NATO or not. And of course, that is a big part of why Russia felt that they were going to intervene. Now, there's nothing that excuses Putin's invasion. It was an unjust invasion of Ukraine. Nothing calls for that. Frankly, all kinds of things are just to repel it. But the question is, should America do those things? And right now, I think what's obvious to a lot of people is that Ukraine does not have the combat power of their own accord. Even if we cut big checks for them and they have technology and weapon systems, they do not have the manpower to extract Russia from all of Ukraine, especially all of Ukraine, including Crimea. So my hope is the part that is said is if we can create a framework that acknowledges these things, then there's a possibility that we would be open to a negotiated settlement. And at the end of the day, that decision really is Ukraine's. But it is also our decision as to what we're going to fund and not fund. Just as it was France's decision when they helped fund our own revolution and separation from you know, from Great Britain. You know, thankfully we got our own country and France was generous to help us. They weren't necessarily obligated to, but you know, we would have had a hard time winning without the support they gave us. And reality is Ukraine has done the fighting, but you know, we've done a lot of funding and we've done a lot of equipping as have some of our allies in Europe and around the world. And so hopefully Ukraine can make the most of that and create something that is defensible, and it has security, it has governance, and it has a strong economy. And if they can do that, then there's a chance for peace.

speaker: SPEAKER_02
transcript: Well, certainly I've introduced the Define the Mission Act in the House. Got a lot of good co-sponsors in the House. Senator Mike Lee carried the Senate companion to it. And this is a restatement of the vote that we had on the National Defense Authorization last July. I referenced that earlier in our conversation. We got 129 votes on that. And that was just limiting, limiting a little bit of funding that goes through NATO. and DOD. So in this case, you're talking about the whole ball of wax, but before we give them another dime, there's nothing someone in Ukraine can answer for this. It has to be our own administration. Tell us the mission. And the response to the letters, a big accelerant of that. Frankly, my colleague, Mike Garcia, Naval Academy Navy fighter pilot, he had put a kind of booklet together that, you know, used a negotiation with the administration and build a coalition of some of the defense hawks to kind of push the same narrative and say, well, we're probably not going to get the law passed that Davidson's asking for, but I essentially have the same question. What is the mission? So you go to the point of the 18% who have served in our military, we're used to saying that upfront, like, what is the mission? What do you want me to accomplish? And so I think that hasn't even been answered. That hasn't stopped the Senate apparently from moving forward with plans to fund it. But I do think it's going to stop the House from even remotely considering it. And when we do agree on the mission, or some consensus comes together to do that, it may be included in some part of our funding for our government. But again, I don't think the House is likely to bring it up unless we commit to secure our own borders and we fund our own government. I think there's just not going to be the votes from the majority party anyway to put it to the floor unless we can say we funded America and we're willing to defend America.
